sources.title: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy (Green-top Guideline No. 21)

indications: Tubal ectopic pregnancy requiring surgery under NICE NG126: rupture, significant pain, adnexal mass of 35 mm or more, visible fetal heartbeat, or hCG of 5000 IU/L or more.
Failed medical management or a woman who chooses surgery.
Salpingectomy when the contralateral tube is healthy; salpingotomy is considered when there are risk factors for infertility.
contraindications: Haemodynamic collapse where laparoscopy would delay control and the surgeon is not experienced: perform laparotomy.
Interstitial, cornual, cervical or caesarean scar pregnancy, which need specialist techniques.
preparation: Group and crossmatch, full blood count, hCG, rhesus status.
Consent including conversion to laparotomy, salpingotomy versus salpingectomy, bleeding, injury to bowel, bladder or vessels, and the effect on fertility.
Ask the woman her wishes about the pregnancy tissue, and offer bereavement support information.
positioning: Supine or Lloyd-Davies with arms tucked, for Trendelenburg tilt; a uterine manipulator is optional and only if intrauterine pregnancy has been excluded.
equipment: Laparoscopy set with 10 mm umbilical and two or three 5 mm ports, high-flow suction irrigation, bipolar energy or a sealing device, endoloops, retrieval bag.
Laparotomy set opened in theatre for the unstable woman.
anatomy: The tube runs in the upper border of the broad ligament from the cornu to the fimbria, supplied by the mesosalpinx between the uterine and ovarian vessels.
Most ectopic pregnancies are ampullary; isthmic and interstitial ones bleed more and rupture earlier.
The ovarian vessels in the infundibulopelvic ligament and the ureter crossing the pelvic brim lie close to the fimbrial end.
criticalSafety: In the shocked woman the first goal is to control bleeding: clamp or grasp the mesosalpinx before evacuating clot.
Divide the mesosalpinx close to the tube to preserve ovarian blood supply.
Use a bag for removal and inspect the specimen for products of conception.
structuresAtRisk: Inferior epigastric vessels at lateral ports
commonErrors: Spending time suctioning blood in an unstable woman before controlling the bleeding source.
Dividing the mesosalpinx too close to the ovary.
Removing the wrong tube after failing to inspect both sides.
Not measuring the haemoperitoneum, so the blood loss is under-reported.
complications: Haemorrhage and need for transfusion or conversion.
Persistent trophoblast, particularly after salpingotomy, needing hCG follow-up.
Injury to bowel, bladder, ureter or vessels.
postop: After salpingectomy with a healthy contralateral tube, a urine pregnancy test at three weeks per NICE NG126; after salpingotomy, serial serum hCG.
Advice on future pregnancy: early scan in the next pregnancy to confirm location.

steps.emphasis: Confirm side from imaging if known, but the side is confirmed at laparoscopy, not marked on the skin.
State the haemodynamic status, blood available and the conversion plan.
Steep Trendelenburg to lift bowel out of the pelvis; confirm the woman is secured before tilting.
Catheterise first. The anaesthetist should expect a fall in blood pressure as pneumoperitoneum is established in a hypovolaemic woman.
Find the bleeding tube first; a full survey follows once bleeding is controlled.
The contralateral tube determines fertility counselling and is the basis for salpingectomy over salpingotomy.
Bag the tube; trophoblast left in the abdomen can implant and persist.
Irrigate the pelvis and inspect the mesosalpinx stump at low pressure.
Count the haemoperitoneum evacuated as blood loss.
Send for histology to confirm trophoblast; record the woman's wishes about the tissue.
NICE NG126 advises anti-D for rhesus-negative women having surgical management of an ectopic pregnancy.

step.salp.control.title: Controlling the bleeding and evacuating haemoperitoneum
step.salp.control.why: In a ruptured ectopic the bleeding source is small and accessible. Grasping it first stops the haemorrhage; suctioning first only measures it.
how: Identify the affected tube, lift it with an atraumatic grasper and hold it to tamponade the mesosalpinx.
Then evacuate clot and blood with high-flow suction and irrigation to clear the field.
Inspect the ectopic site: ampullary, isthmic, fimbrial, or interstitial (which changes the plan).
pitfalls: Suctioning for minutes before grasping the tube in an unstable woman.
Missing an interstitial ectopic and treating it as ampullary.

step.salp.excise.title: Salpingectomy
step.salp.excise.why: Removing the tube with its pregnancy is definitive and avoids persistent trophoblast. Staying close to the tube protects the ovarian supply.
how: Starting at the fimbrial end or the isthmus, coagulate and divide the mesosalpinx close to the tube in short steps.
Divide the tube at the isthmus close to the cornu.
Alternatively, place sequential endoloops around the tube and mesosalpinx before excision.
If salpingotomy is chosen instead, make a linear antimesenteric incision over the ectopic, remove it, achieve haemostasis, and arrange serial hCG.
pitfalls: Leaving a long tubal stump at the fimbrial end.
